  class.output = "spax-output",

```

spax computes two kinds of result from the same demand, supply and travel
times. A floating catchment area (FCA) index measures how much supply a place
has relative to the demand that competes for it. An allocation model says
where the residents of a place go: a probability for each facility and for an
outside option, which stands for every choice outside the facilities in the
data. Its parameters are fitted to the use you observed. This guide computes
both for the same small areas and sets them side by side, so that you can
choose the one that answers your question. It uses the GP registrations, practices and
travel times of [The Cornwall GP example data](cornwall-data.html). The
`spax()` interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change in
later versions.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Which one answers your question?

Start from the quantity you need and the observations you have.

| Question | Call | What you get |
|:--|:--|:--|
| How much supply does each place have, relative to the demand that can reach it? | `spax(data, spec_e2sfca())`, or another FCA specification: `spec_2sfca()`, `spec_m2sfca()`, `spec_3sfca()`, `spec_huff2sfca()` | An index of supply per travel-weighted resident |
| Where do residents go, among the facilities and an outside option? | `spax(data, spec_clm(decay_gaussian(sigma = 5), outside = 0.03))`, with a value for every parameter | A probability for each facility and the outside option, and the expected number of users of each facility |
| Which parameters fit the use you observed? | `spax(data, spec_clm(), observed = obs_flows())`, or `obs_totals()` for facility totals | Fitted parameters, read with `coef()` and checked with `check_fit()` |
| What changes when supply changes, at the same parameters? | `spax()` on the changed data, with the fitted values held | The difference between two modeled scenarios |
| What does the model give at other places? | `predict()` on the fitted result | Probabilities and outside shares at those places |
| How sure are the estimates? | `bootstrap_fit()` on an allocation model with a fitted outside weight, fitted to facility totals | Bootstrap intervals for the parameters and for a scenario |

An FCA index needs no observations, and the analyst chooses how fast its
weights fall with travel time. An allocation model can be fitted to observed
counts, and its fitted counts can then be checked against them.

## One Cornwall system, two calculations

Both calculations below use the same inputs for mainland Cornwall: small
areas and their GP practices. Demand is the number of residents of each area
registered with a GP practice, and supply is each practice's GP full-time
equivalents (FTE), excluding GPs in training. Travel is a matrix of minutes
from each area to each practice. `prep_data()` lines the three up by their
IDs, and `obs_flows()` declares the observed registrations by area and
practice.

```{r inputs}
areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")
d
```

The prepared data hold `r nrow(areas)` small areas (lower layer super output
areas, LSOAs) and `r nrow(gp)` practices. spax calls the small areas origins
and the practices facilities, in the print and in its tables. The unit labels
are kept with the data and every result, and spax does not convert units.

### An FCA index

The enhanced two-step floating catchment area method (E2SFCA) works in two
steps. Each practice divides its supply by the demand that can reach it,
weighted by travel time. Each area then adds up the ratios of the practices
it can reach, with the same weights. Here the weight of a practice $d$
minutes away is $w(d) = \exp(-d^2 / 2\sigma^2)$, a Gaussian curve with a
travel scale σ of 10 minutes, so a practice 10 minutes away counts with weight
`r round(exp(-1 / 2), 2)`. The 10 minutes is a choice for this guide. With
small areas as the origins, `spax()` returns one value per area. On a
population grid it returns a map. `as.data.frame()` gives one row per area,
with the index in a column named after the supply layer, `supply`.

```{r fca}
# The E2SFCA index at each area, with a 10-minute Gaussian decay
fca <- spax(d, spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))
fca

# One row per area. The index column is named after the supply layer;
# times 1,000 it is in GP FTE per 1,000 travel-weighted registered residents
fca_index <- as.data.frame(fca) |>
  transmute(lsoa = origin_id, fca = 1000 * supply)
summary(fca_index$fca)
```

The index ranges from `r round(min(fca_index$fca), 2)` to
`r round(max(fca_index$fca), 2)` GP FTE per 1,000 travel-weighted registered
residents across the areas. The print lists one layer, `supply`: with several
supply measures, such as GP FTE with and without GPs in training, each gives a
layer and an index of its own. `normalize identity` means that demand is used
as it is.

### An allocation model fitted to registrations

The conditional logit model (CLM) gives each practice an attraction: its GP
FTE times a decay weight of the travel time. It adds an outside option with a
weight v0 of its own. The residents of area $i$ go to practice $j$ with
probability

$$P_{ij} = \frac{S_j\, w(d_{ij})}{\sum_k S_k\, w(d_{ik}) + v_0},$$

where $S_j$ is the practice's supply and $w(d_{ij})$ the decay weight of the
travel time $d_{ij}$. They go to the outside option with the remaining
probability.
Here the outside option stands for registration with a practice outside
mainland Cornwall, in Devon for example. `spec_clm()` declares the model
with a Gaussian decay, and by default `spax()` fits both the travel scale σ and
the outside weight v0. Fitting searches for the values whose expected
registrations (demand times probability) come closest to the observed counts,
as measured by a Poisson loss.

```{r clm}
# Gaussian decay and outside weight, both fitted to the registrations
clm <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows)
clm
```

```{r clm-values, include = FALSE}
sigma_hat <- round(coef(clm)[["sigma"]], 1)
v0_hat <- signif(coef(clm)[["v0"]], 2)
clm_starts <- as.data.frame(clm, type = "starts")
# The text says that every search converged
stopifnot(all(clm_starts$eligible))
```

The message about the Isles of Scilly is explained in [Where do residents
register?](allocation-workflow.html#fit-the-model). In the print, `beta` and
`kappa` shape the attraction. Both are held at 1, so the
attraction is the GP FTE itself, as in the formula. No starting values were
given, so `spax()` evaluated the loss on a grid of σ and v0 values and started
the search from `r nrow(clm_starts)` of them. Each of the
`r nrow(clm_starts)` searches converged, and `spax()` kept the best fit.

The fitted travel scale σ is about `r sigma_hat` minutes, much shorter than
the 10 minutes chosen for the FCA index: registration is very local. The
outside weight v0 is on the scale of an attraction: `r v0_hat` is the pull of
a practice with that many GP FTE next door. So the outside option matters only
where every practice is far away.

## What one area sees

The two calculations weight the same practices in different ways. Take the
area with the largest total FCA weight, one with many practices within a short
drive. `predict()` gives the CLM's probabilities for every area, and the
fit's flow table gives the registrations by area and practice. The table
lists the practices within 7 minutes of the area. `clm_prob` is the CLM
probability and `obs_share` the observed share of the area's registered
residents.

```{r one-area}
# CLM probabilities for every area and practice, and outside shares
prediction <- predict(clm, travel, demand,
  outputs = c("allocation", "outside_share"))
probability <- prediction$outputs$allocation

# Registrations by area (rows) and practice (columns), from the flow table
flow_table <- as.data.frame(clm, type = "flows")
observed <- xtabs(observed ~ origin_id + facility_id, flow_table)
observed <- observed[rownames(travel), colnames(travel)]

# The FCA's Gaussian weights, with the 10-minute travel scale
fca_weight <- exp(-travel^2 / (2 * 10^2))

# The area with the largest total FCA weight, and the practices within 7 minutes
area <- which.max(rowSums(fca_weight))
nearest <- order(travel[area, ])
nearest <- nearest[travel[area, nearest] <= 7]

data.frame(
  practice = tools::toTitleCase(tolower(gp$name[nearest])),
  gp_fte = round(supply[nearest], 1),
  minutes = travel[area, nearest],
  fca_weight = round(fca_weight[area, nearest], 2),
  clm_prob = round(probability[area, nearest], 3),
  obs_share = round(observed[area, nearest] / demand[area], 3),
  row.names = NULL
)

# Totals over all practices for this area
round(
  c(
    fca_weights = sum(fca_weight[area, ]),
    clm_practices = sum(probability[area, ]),
    clm_outside = prediction$outputs$outside_share[[area]]
  ),
  4
)
```

```{r one-area-values, include = FALSE}
# The sentence below compares Lander (L82001) with Chacewater (L82015)
lander <- "L82001"
chacewater <- "L82015"
stopifnot(
  travel[area, lander] > travel[area, chacewater],
  probability[area, lander] > probability[area, chacewater],
  # ... and quotes the observed and modeled shares at the single nearest practice
  travel[area, nearest[1]] < travel[area, nearest[2]]
)
```

The FCA weights are separate discounts, one per practice. They do not compete
with each other, and for this area they add up to
`r round(sum(fca_weight[area, ]), 1)`, as much weight as
`r round(sum(fca_weight[area, ]))` practices next door. The CLM probabilities
compete: a nearby practice with more GP FTE draws residents away from the
others, and the probabilities over all practices and the outside option add up
to 1. Lander Medical Practice, `r travel[area, lander]` minutes away with
`r round(supply[[lander]], 1)` GP FTE, gets a higher probability than
Chacewater Health Centre, `r travel[area, chacewater]` minutes away with
`r round(supply[[chacewater]], 1)` GP FTE.

Because they are probabilities, they can be set beside the observed shares. At
this one area they differ markedly:
`r round(100 * observed[area, nearest[1]] / demand[area])`% of residents are
registered at the nearest practice, against a modeled
`r round(100 * probability[area, nearest[1]])`%. The model knows only travel
time and GP FTE, so the next section judges it across all areas.

## Side by side

The FCA index gives one value per area. The CLM gives each area a
distribution over the practices, and other quantities follow from it:
expected registrations (demand times probability), each practice's expected
list (the residents registered with it: its expected registrations summed over
areas) and the mean travel time to the practice an area's residents are
modeled to register with. The maps show the FCA index and that
mean travel time.

```{r maps, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "49%", fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = c("Map of mainland Cornwall's small areas colored by the E2SFCA index with a 10-minute Gaussian decay, in GP FTE per 1,000 travel-weighted registered residents; it is lowest at the western tip, on the Lizard peninsula and on the north coast around Padstow, and highest in a few central and eastern areas.", "Map of mainland Cornwall's small areas colored by the CLM's mean travel time, in minutes, to the practice that residents are modeled to register with; the longest times are on the north coast around Padstow, in the rural north-east and at the western tip.")}
# The FCA index and the CLM's probability-weighted mean minutes per area
areas <- areas |>
  left_join(fca_index, by = "lsoa") |>
  mutate(clm_minutes = rowSums(probability * travel) / rowSums(probability))

# Join to the small-area polygons for mapping
mapped <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  select(lsoa) |>
  inner_join(areas, by = "lsoa")

ggplot(mapped) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = fca, color = fca), linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(mapped), fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "GP FTE\nper 1,000",
    aesthetics = c("fill", "color")
  ) +
  labs(title = "E2SFCA index (sigma = 10 min)") +
  theme_void()

ggplot(mapped) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = clm_minutes, color = clm_minutes), linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(mapped), fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Minutes",
    option = "magma",
    direction = -1,
    aesthetics = c("fill", "color")
  ) +
  labs(title = "CLM: mean minutes to modeled practice") +
  theme_void()
```

```{r map-values, include = FALSE}
# Bude, in the far north-east: the small areas Cornwall 001A to 001F
bude <- startsWith(areas$name, "Cornwall 001")
r_maps <- sprintf("%.2f", cor(areas$fca, areas$clm_minutes))
stopifnot(
  sum(bude) == 6,
  all(areas$fca[bude] < quantile(areas$fca, 0.25))
)
```

In both maps darker means less favorable: a lower index, or a longer modeled
trip. Both are dark at the western tip, on the north coast around Padstow and
inland in the north-east. Elsewhere they can part. In Bude, in the far
north-east, the modeled trips are short, at most
`r ceiling(max(areas$clm_minutes[bude]))` minutes, yet the index is in the
lowest quarter of areas: few GP FTE lie within reach of the residents who
share them. Across areas, a higher index goes with shorter modeled trips only
loosely: the two correlate at `r r_maps`.

The CLM's fitted registrations can be compared with the observed ones. The FCA
index has no observed counterpart in these data.

```{r check}
# Correlations of modeled with observed: area mean minutes, practice lists
observed_minutes <- rowSums(observed * travel) / rowSums(observed)
c(
  mean_minutes = cor(areas$clm_minutes, observed_minutes),
  practice_lists = cor(colSums(fitted(clm)), colSums(observed))
)

# Share of residents registered outside mainland Cornwall (%), observed and
# modeled
outside <- c(
  observed = 1 - sum(observed) / sum(demand),
  modeled = 1 - sum(fitted(clm)) / sum(demand)
)
round(100 * outside, 2)
```

```{r check-values, include = FALSE}
r_minutes <- sprintf("%.2f", cor(areas$clm_minutes, observed_minutes))
r_lists <- sprintf("%.2f", cor(colSums(fitted(clm)), colSums(observed)))
```

Modeled and observed mean travel times correlate at `r r_minutes` across
areas, and modeled and observed practice lists at `r r_lists`. The model puts
fewer residents outside mainland Cornwall than observed
(`r round(100 * outside[["modeled"]], 2)`% against
`r round(100 * outside[["observed"]], 2)`%). This fit uses only the counts at
mainland practices, so nothing ties its outside total to the observed one.

Declared as known, the outside counts make the two totals agree: see [When
outside counts are known](allocation-workflow.html#when-outside-counts-are-known).
Even then, one outside weight for every area cannot reproduce where
registration outside mainland Cornwall happens: mostly in a few areas near the
Devon border, as the outside-option map in [Where do residents
register?](allocation-workflow.html#the-outside-option) shows.

Use an FCA index when you need supply relative to demand, have no counts of
where people go, or want a decay you set yourself. Use the allocation model
when you need to know where residents go, have counts to fit it to, and want
to check it against them.

| | E2SFCA index | CLM |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Per area | One supply-per-demand value for each supply measure | A probability for each practice and for the outside option |
| Supply | Each supply measure gives its own index | One supply measure, which sets the attraction and does not cap the list |
| Travel decay | Chosen by the analyst (10 minutes here) | Fitted to the registrations (about `r sigma_hat` minutes here) |
| Outside option | None | A weight v0, fitted here |
| Check against registrations | No observed counterpart | Fitted registrations, practice lists and outside share |

[Reading results](reading-results.html) says what each output measures.
